idiom_name: hand-built handle table: opaque handle + ops table, wrapper handles, and a membrane table
implementation_notes: C has no objects, no reflection and no way to intercept a call, so the membrane has to be built on an object model you define yourself: represent every reference as an opaque handle (an index or pointer into a registry) whose object carries a table of function pointers, and represent the membrane as a second registry that maps a handle to its wrapper handle plus the membrane's policy. Every API entry point on a handle can then wrap the arguments, dispatch to the wrapped target and wrap the result, which is the whole pattern; the identity map is a hash table keyed on the target handle, and revocation is a flag or generation counter checked in one place. The structure is fully hand-written, and it holds only for code that goes through the handle API: C pointers are forgeable and dereferenceable, so any path that hands out or accepts a raw pointer (a captured callback context, a struct field, shared memory) can bypass the membrane, and the guarantee is a discipline rather than an enforcement. Real capability systems show the shape at its strongest - a file descriptor is a process-local handle and cap_rights_limit() reduces the rights attached to one, after which the kernel filters every operation on that descriptor, which is a membrane implemented by the operating system instead of by convention.
pitfalls: The membrane holds only for code that goes through the handle API: any raw obj * that escapes (a struct field, a captured callback argument, a shared buffer) is a route around it, and C cannot prevent the escape.

Handles must be validated on every entry: an unchecked index, a stale pointer or a freed handle can be turned into a reference to an object that was never wrapped, which is exactly the bypass the pattern exists to prevent.
The membrane table is mutable shared state: without a lock or a per-membrane generation counter, wrapping and revocation race, and a handle wrapped after revocation stays live.
